Ashokan edictsDhammaBrahmi scriptEpigraphic sources

The inscriptions of Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE) are the earliest deciphered written records of Indian history. Engraved on rocks, polished pillars and cave walls from Afghanistan to Karnataka, most are in Prakrit written in the Brahmi script, which James Prinsep deciphered in 1837. Because they speak in the emperor's own voice ("Devanampiya Piyadasi"), they are a first-hand source on the Mauryas.

1. Political history and extent of the empire

  • Find-spots mark the frontiers: edicts at Shahbazgarhi (Pakistan), Kandahar (Afghanistan), Kalsi, Girnar, Dhauli, Erragudi (Andhra Pradesh) and Brahmagiri (Karnataka) outline an empire from the Hindu Kush to the Deccan.
  • Kalinga war: Rock Edict XIII records the conquest of Kalinga eight years after Ashoka's consecration, with 1,50,000 people deported and 1,00,000 killed, and his remorse; Rock Edict IV says the sound of the war drum gave way to the sound of Dhamma.
  • Neighbours and diplomacy: Rock Edicts II and XIII name the southern kingdoms (Cholas, Pandyas, Keralaputras), Sri Lanka and five Greek kings such as Antiochus II and Ptolemy II, whose known dates help fix Mauryan chronology.
  • Identity of the king: the Maski edict (found in 1915) first gave the name "Asoka", linking the Piyadasi of the edicts with the Ashoka of the chronicles.

2. Administration and the policy of Dhamma

  • Officials: rajukas, pradesikas and yuktas toured every five years (Rock Edict III); Dhamma Mahamattas were appointed in the thirteenth regnal year (Rock Edict V).
  • Paternal kingship: the Separate Kalinga Edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada declare that "all men are my children".
  • Justice and welfare: Pillar Edict IV gave condemned prisoners a three-day respite; other edicts mention medical care for humans and animals, wells and roadside trees.
  • Ethics of Dhamma: tolerance of all sects (Rock Edict XII), respect for elders, kindness to slaves and servants, and a ban on animal sacrifice (Rock Edict I).

3. Religion, economy, society and culture

  • Buddhism: the Bairat (Bhabru) edict names Buddhist texts; the Schism Edict warns monks against splitting the Sangha.
  • Rare economic data: the Rummindei pillar records Ashoka's visit to Lumbini, which he exempted from bali and whose share of produce (bhaga) he cut to one-eighth.
  • Patronage of all sects: the Barabar caves were gifted to the Ajivikas.
  • A multilingual empire and its art: Kharosthi in the north-west and Greek and Aramaic at Kandahar show adaptation to local scripts; the Sarnath lion capital is India's national emblem.

4. Limitations

  • Royal voice: the edicts state the king's ideals, not how far they were enforced.
  • Silences: little on his predecessors, trade or the empire's decline; dates are given only in regnal years.
  • Need for corroboration: they must be read with the Arthashastra, the Indica, the Buddhist chronicles and archaeology.

In sum, the inscriptions turn Mauryan history from legend into documented history, revealing an empire's extent and administration and an early experiment in ethical governance.
free.upm-2026-gs1-2:
Macaulay's Minute (1835)Anglicist–Orientalist debateDownward filtrationEnglish education

Thomas Babington Macaulay, the Law Member of the Governor-General's Council, wrote his Minute on Indian Education on 2 February 1835. It settled the Anglicist–Orientalist controversy over how to spend the one lakh rupees a year set aside for education by the Charter Act of 1813, arguing for English and Western science instead of Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian learning. Lord William Bentinck's resolution of 7 March 1835 accepted it.

1. What the Minute proposed

  • English as the medium: government funds were to support English schools and colleges, not oriental printing and stipends.
  • Contempt for Indian learning: Macaulay claimed that "a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia".
  • A class of interpreters: he wanted "a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect" to stand between the rulers and the ruled.
  • Downward filtration: educating a small upper class, it was assumed, would spread knowledge to the masses through the vernaculars.

2. Impact on colonial administration

  • Language of power: after 1837 English replaced Persian in higher administration and courts, with vernaculars in the lower courts.
  • A cheap subordinate bureaucracy: Hardinge's resolution (1844) made English the passport to government jobs, producing clerks, translators and lawyers who ran the Raj at low cost.
  • Uniform, codified rule: the same Anglicist outlook shaped Macaulay's draft of the Indian Penal Code (enacted 1860) and his 1854 report on a competitive ICS examination, held in London in English, which kept Indians at a disadvantage.

3. Impact on education

  • Western knowledge: English schools and colleges spread science, history and political thought; Wood's Despatch and the universities of 1857 built on this base.
  • Neglect of mass education: filtration did not reach the masses, and literacy was only about 18% even in 1951.
  • Decline of indigenous learning: pathshalas, madrasas and tols lost patronage, and Sanskrit and Persian scholarship shrank.
  • Elite–mass gap and rote learning: an English-knowing elite drifted away from the people, and education became exam-oriented and job-centred.

4. Unintended consequences

  • A modern middle class: English-educated Indians led social reform and founded the Indian National Congress (1885).
  • Weapons against the Raj: ideas of liberty, democracy and nationalism were turned against colonial rule.
  • A link language: English connected an all-India intelligentsia and press, even as Indian-language literature also flourished.

Macaulay's Minute thus left a dual legacy: it served colonial administration but also created the class that challenged it. The NEP 2020 emphasis on teaching in the mother tongue wherever possible, at least up to Class 5 and preferably till Class 8, seeks to balance English with Indian languages.

Self-identificationArticle 21 privacyTransgender Persons ActMedical certification

In NALSA v. Union of India (2014) the Supreme Court recognised transgender persons as a "third gender" and held that the right to self-identify one's gender flows from dignity and personal liberty under Article 21. K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) made privacy, including bodily and decisional autonomy, a fundamental right. The 2019 Act gave a "right to self-perceived gender identity" (Section 4(2)); the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026 (assented to on 30 March 2026) replaces self-identification with medical verification.

1. What the 2026 amendment changes

  • Narrower definition: a transgender person now means persons with socio-cultural identities such as kinner, hijra, aravani and jogta, persons with intersex variations, and persons compelled by force or deceit to assume a transgender identity; persons with different sexual orientations and self-perceived identities are expressly excluded.
  • Self-identification removed: Section 4(2) is deleted, so trans men, trans women and genderqueer persons outside these groups lose recognition under the Act.
  • Medical gatekeeping: the District Magistrate issues a certificate of identity only after examining the recommendation of a medical board (the "authority") headed by the Chief Medical Officer, and hospitals must report gender-affirming surgery to the District Magistrate and the board.
  • Harsher penalties: the 2019 offences (such as denying access to public places or forcing a person out of home) keep six months to two years; new offences carry 10 years to life for kidnapping and grievous hurt to force a transgender identity on an adult (life if a child), and 5 to 10 years for compelling such a person into begging or servitude.

2. Effect on privacy and self-identity

  • Departure from NALSA: NALSA treated gender identity as a deeply felt internal experience, not a biological test; making a medical board the judge reverses this.
  • Bodily privacy: a compulsory examination intrudes on bodily integrity and decisional autonomy protected in Puttaswamy, and exposes intimate data to officials.
  • Equality and welfare: persons left out of the definition may lose access to the National Portal for Transgender Persons, the SMILE scheme and Garima Greh shelters, raising concerns under Articles 14, 15 and 19(1)(a) (expression of gender).
  • Retrospective doubt: the words "nor shall ever have been so included" may unsettle certificates already issued.
  • Chilling effect: broad criminal clauses may deter doctors from offering gender-affirming care.

3. The government's rationale and the proportionality test

  • Preventing misuse: verification is meant to ensure that welfare and affirmative action reach genuine beneficiaries.
  • Protection: harsher penalties target forced castration, trafficking and forced begging, which are real harms.
  • Proportionality: under the Puttaswamy test the aim is legitimate, but a less intrusive tool, such as a sworn self-declaration with penalties for fraud, may achieve it.

In May 2026 the Supreme Court issued notice on petitions challenging the amendment but did not stay it. Keeping self-determination at the core, with light-touch safeguards against fraud, would honour both dignity and the State's legitimate interest.
free.upm-2026-gs2-2:
Article 15(3)73rd and 74th Amendments106th AmendmentSubstantive equality

Women are neither a numerical minority nor a caste-based backward class, so their claim to reservation rests not on Articles 15(4) and 16(4) but on Article 15(3), which permits special provisions for women, and on the idea of substantive equality. That is why women's quotas are horizontal: they cut across SC, ST, OBC and general categories. Their journey has run from panchayats (1992) to Parliament (2023), though no legislative seat has yet been reserved.

1. Why reservation became necessary

  • Under-representation: women were under 5% of the first Lok Sabha and are only about 14% of the 18th Lok Sabha (2024).
  • Structural barriers: patriarchy, care burdens, costly elections and party gatekeeping keep women off candidate lists.
  • Early reluctance: women members of the Constituent Assembly such as Renuka Ray opposed reserved seats, trusting adult franchise and equal citizenship.
  • Towards Equality (1974): the Committee on the Status of Women in India exposed women's political marginalisation and proposed statutory women's panchayats, though its majority did not favour reserved seats in legislatures.

2. Local bodies: from experiment to constitutional mandate

  • State initiatives: Karnataka's 1983 panchayat law reserved 25% of seats for women, and the National Perspective Plan for Women (1988) proposed 30% in local bodies.
  • 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992): at least one-third of seats and of panchayat chairpersons' posts (Article 243D), and one-third of municipal seats (Article 243T), including one-third of the seats reserved for SCs and STs.
  • Beyond one-third: Bihar became the first State to reserve 50% of panchayat seats (2006); 21 States and two UTs now do so, and women hold nearly half of all panchayat seats.
  • Limits: proxy rule by husbands ("sarpanch-pati"), rotation of seats every term and weak devolution dilute real power.

3. Parliament and Assemblies: a long wait

  • Failed attempts: the 81st Amendment Bill (1996), examined by the Geeta Mukherjee Committee, and later versions lapsed; the 108th Amendment Bill passed the Rajya Sabha in 2010 but lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha in 2014.
  • 106th Amendment (2023), the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam: reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly (Articles 330A, 332A, 239AA), including within SC and ST seats, for 15 years, with rotation after each delimitation.
  • Conditional start (Article 334A): it takes effect only after a delimitation based on the first Census taken after the Act's commencement. The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, which sought earlier implementation through a delimitation based on the 2011 Census, with the Lok Sabha enlarged to up to 850 seats, was defeated in the Lok Sabha on 17 April 2026: it got 298 votes to 230, short of the 352 (two-thirds of members present and voting) required.
  • Gaps: there is no OBC sub-quota and no reservation in the Rajya Sabha or the Legislative Councils.

Women's leadership in local bodies has created a pool of experienced women politicians; implementing legislative reservation through political consensus on delimitation would turn formal equality into substantive representation.
free.upm-2026-gs3-1:
Digital Rupee (e₹)Central Bank Digital CurrencyTwo-tier distributionProgrammable money

The Digital Rupee (e₹) is India's Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC): legal tender issued by the Reserve Bank of India in digital form. Like a currency note, it is a direct liability of the RBI and is exchangeable one-to-one with cash, so it carries no credit risk. The RBI Act, 1934 was amended through the Finance Act, 2022 to allow it, and the RBI's Concept Note (October 2022) set out its design.

1. What the Digital Rupee is

  • Sovereign money, not bank money: a UPI payment moves a bank deposit, whereas e₹ moves the RBI's own money from wallet to wallet; settlement is final.
  • Two variants: wholesale e₹-W for settling large inter-bank transactions (pilot from 1 November 2022) and retail e₹-R for people and merchants (pilot from 1 December 2022).
  • Not a cryptocurrency: it has a central issuer and a stable value, unlike private crypto assets, which India taxes but does not treat as legal tender.

2. Working of India's CBDC

  • Two-tier model: the RBI creates and issues e₹; authorised banks distribute it to customers' digital wallets and handle KYC, so the RBI does not deal with the public directly.
  • Token-based retail e₹: each token behaves like a note or coin; a user loads the wallet from a bank account and pays persons or merchants by scanning a QR code, including UPI QR codes.
  • Account-based wholesale e₹: banks settle large-value transactions; their balances are redeemed into current accounts at the end of the day.
  • New features: programmability (money usable only for a set purpose), offline payments for areas with weak connectivity, and a sandbox for fintech firms to test products.

3. Progress so far

  • Scale: over 80 lakh users and more than 12 crore retail transactions worth over ₹28,000 crore (RBI Deputy Governor, December 2025).
  • Circulation: retail e₹ in circulation fell about 24% to ₹771.7 crore at end-March 2026 from ₹1,016.5 crore a year earlier (RBI Annual Report 2025-26), a sign that UPI already meets most needs.
  • Programmable welfare: food subsidy was paid as programmable CBDC to PDS beneficiaries in Gujarat, Puducherry and Chandigarh, redeemable only for eligible goods at fair price shops.
  • Wholesale and tokenisation: tokenised certificates of deposit are being piloted with wholesale CBDC settlement.
  • Cross-border: an MoU with Singapore's central bank and BIS projects (Rialto, Mandala); cross-border pilots are planned for 2026-27.

4. Challenges

  • Low adoption: free, instant UPI leaves users little reason to switch.
  • Privacy: fears of transaction tracking call for strong safeguards under the DPDP Act, 2023.
  • Bank disintermediation: a large shift of deposits into e₹ could hurt bank lending; hence it pays no interest.

The e₹ is a calibrated, pilot-led reform. Its future lies less in competing with UPI than in programmable welfare, offline payments and cheaper cross-border settlement.
free.upm-2026-gs3-2:
Financial inclusionInclusive growthJAM trinityFI-Index

The Rangarajan Committee (2008) defined financial inclusion as access to financial services, and timely and adequate credit, for vulnerable groups such as weaker sections and low-income groups at an affordable cost. Where most workers are informal, exclusion from finance traps households in moneylender debt, so inclusion is a building block of inclusive growth, not merely a banking goal.

1. An integral part of economic inclusion

  • Credit for livelihoods: Mudra loans (2015), Stand-Up India, PM SVANidhi (2020) and SHG–bank linkage give small borrowers working capital and reduce dependence on moneylenders.
  • Savings and assets: PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014) has over 59 crore accounts with about ₹3.17 lakh crore in deposits (August 2026).
  • Risk protection: PMJJBY, PMSBY and the Atal Pension Yojana (2015) protect families from falling back into poverty after a death, accident or old age.
  • Formalisation: digital payments build credit histories that enable collateral-free loans to MSMEs and street vendors.

2. An integral part of social inclusion

  • Women's agency: about 56% of Jan Dhan accounts belong to women, and SHGs under DAY-NRLM (about 10 crore women) give them savings, credit and a voice.
  • Direct Benefit Transfer: the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) delivers scholarships, pensions and PM-KISAN directly, cutting out middlemen who exploit the poor.
  • Reach: 78% of Jan Dhan accounts are in rural or semi-urban areas; business correspondents and the India Post Payments Bank (2018) serve remote, tribal and hill villages.
  • Necessary but not sufficient: dormant accounts, low use of credit and insurance, and digital fraud show that access alone is not inclusion; the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis (2010) showed that credit without safeguards can deepen distress.

3. RBI's Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index)

  • Design: launched in August 2021 and published annually, it scores inclusion from 0 (complete exclusion) to 100 (full inclusion) using 97 indicators across banking, investments, insurance, postal and pension services.
  • Three sub-indices: Access (35%), Usage (45%) and Quality (20%); quality covers financial literacy, consumer protection and deficiencies in services.
  • Trend: the index rose to 70.0 in March 2026 from 67.0 a year earlier, driven mainly by higher usage (RBI, July 2026).

4. Usefulness of the index

  • Measures depth, not just accounts: the heavy weight on usage and quality shifts attention from opening accounts to using them well.
  • Single, comparable measure: it combines banking, insurance, pension, postal and securities services and tracks progress year by year.
  • Guides policy: it shows which dimension lags, helping targets under the National Strategy for Financial Inclusion.
  • Limits: a single national figure does not show which States, social groups or genders are left out, and it relies mostly on supply-side data from institutions.

Financial inclusion is the gateway to social and economic citizenship. The next step is meaningful inclusion: State-level and gender-wise indices, financial literacy and strong protection against digital fraud.
free.upm-2026-gs4-1a:
AccountabilityIntegrityGenerative AIAcademic evaluation

A Ph.D. evaluation is a position of public trust: the examiner certifies, under his own signature, that a thesis is original and worthy of a doctorate. Getting generative AI to write the report and submitting it with a few changes hands the judgement to a machine while the signature stays human. Lack of time may explain it, but it raises questions of accountability (who answers for the verdict?) and integrity (is the professor honest about whose judgement it is?).

1. Accountability: answerability for the verdict

  • Non-delegable duty: the university appointed the professor for his expert judgement. Tools may assist, but the assessment of originality, method and contribution cannot be outsourced; he remains answerable for every line he signs.
  • Risk of error: AI tools can misread data, invent references or give generic praise. A wrong verdict may fail a deserving scholar or pass a weak thesis, and the blame cannot be shifted to software.
  • Confidentiality: uploading an unpublished thesis to a public AI tool may breach the candidate's intellectual property and the university's confidentiality norms; many journals bar reviewers from feeding manuscripts into generative AI for this reason.
  • Answerability to stakeholders: the candidate, the university, the regulator and employers all rely on the report; a degree is only as credible as its evaluation.

2. Integrity: honesty, not mere compliance

  • Misrepresentation: presenting machine-written text as one's own considered opinion is intellectual dishonesty, the very fault examiners must detect under the UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018.
  • Double standard: a professor who would penalise a student for undisclosed AI use cannot use it himself; integrity means consistency between what one demands and what one does.
  • Fairness to the scholar: years of research deserve a careful reading; a shortcut violates the duty of care owed to the candidate.
  • Role model: teachers shape the ethical culture of academia; such conduct normalises shortcuts among future researchers.

3. The right course

  • Honest refusal over dishonest acceptance: heavy workload justifies asking for more time or declining the assignment, not cutting corners.
  • Disclosure: if AI is used for limited support, the university should be told.
  • Institutional policy: universities should frame clear rules for examiners on AI use, in line with the India AI Governance Guidelines (MeitY, November 2025), whose principles include accountability and a people-first approach with human oversight.

AI can assist, but it cannot replace professional judgement: whoever signs a report owns it. Accountability and intellectual honesty require the professor either to evaluate the thesis himself or to decline openly.
free.upm-2026-gs4-1b:
Forest Rights ActDevelopment vs displacementGram sabha consentDistributive justice

Projects that displace forest communities set economic growth against the land, livelihood and culture of some of India's most vulnerable people. As the district's administrative officer, I am expected to facilitate investment, yet I am also the statutory guardian of their rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 (FRA), PESA, 1996 and, in Scheduled Areas, the Fifth Schedule. This dual role creates several ethical challenges.

1. Development versus rights and livelihood

  • Competing goods: the project may bring jobs, revenue and roads; displacement destroys land, forest produce, sacred groves and identity, which cash compensation rarely restores.
  • Legal duty under pressure: under Section 4(5) of the FRA, no forest dweller can be evicted until the recognition and verification of rights is complete. Pressure from the company, and sometimes from above, to speed up clearances will test my integrity.
  • Consent, not mere consultation: in the Niyamgiri case (Orissa Mining Corporation v MoEF, 2013), the Supreme Court left it to the gram sabhas to decide whether bauxite mining would affect their religious and cultural rights, and they rejected it. Ensuring free, uncoerced gram sabha meetings is my duty.

2. Fairness and transparency in the process

  • Information asymmetry: project documents are often technical and in English; honesty requires translation, open public hearings and time to deliberate.
  • Fair compensation: the RFCTLARR Act, 2013 requires a social impact assessment, the consent of 80% of affected families for private projects (70% for PPP projects), rehabilitation and resettlement, and special safeguards for Scheduled Tribes.
  • Avoiding conflict of interest: gifts, hospitality or CSR offers from the business house must not influence official decisions.

3. Compassion and the use of force

  • Temptation of coercion: protests may tempt the use of police force or cases against activists; dialogue and proportionality must come first.
  • The most vulnerable: women, the elderly, PVTGs and families without land records risk being left off compensation lists.
  • Environmental ethics: loss of forest affects wildlife, water and future generations; the state is a trustee of natural resources (public trust doctrine, M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath, 1997).

4. Personal ethical challenges

  • Moral courage: giving an honest report on rights and impacts even if it delays the project, and resisting political or corporate pressure.
  • Empathy with neutrality: sympathy for the community must not turn into bias against legitimate development; I must be fair to both sides.
  • Loyalty versus conscience: if superiors push for shortcuts, I must give frank advice on file rather than silently comply.

The officer must act as a trustee of the community's rights, following the law in letter and spirit, so that development is inclusive: no displacement without settled rights, informed consent and rehabilitation that leaves families better off.
free.upm-2025-gs1-1:
Harappan town planningCitadel and lower townBurnt bricksCovered drains

The Harappan Civilization (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) built South Asia's first planned cities. Excavations at Harappa (Daya Ram Sahni, 1921), Mohenjo-daro (R.D. Banerji, 1922), Kalibangan, Lothal, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi reveal an architecture that was utilitarian rather than monumental: standard bricks, planned streets, covered drains and large public structures, but no clearly identified palace or temple.

1. Town planning

  • Grid layout: main streets ran north–south and east–west and crossed at right angles, dividing the town into rectangular blocks; narrow lanes led into the residential quarters.
  • Citadel and lower town: a raised, walled citadel on the west held public buildings, while a larger lower town to the east housed the people. Dholavira had a three-fold division into citadel, middle town and lower town.
  • Walls and platforms: settlements were fortified, and buildings stood on raised mud-brick platforms, partly as protection against floods.

2. Materials and houses

  • Standardised bricks: burnt bricks in the uniform ratio 1:2:4 were used over a vast area, showing common standards of measurement; Kalibangan used mud bricks and Dholavira mainly stone.
  • Courtyard houses: one or two storeys built around an open courtyard, with wells, bathrooms and kitchens; doors opened into side lanes rather than main streets, ensuring privacy.
  • Social differences: houses ranged from small two-room dwellings to large mansions, and rows of small single-room units near the Harappa granaries are often read as workers' quarters.
  • Plain style: walls were plain, with little ornament; the true arch was unknown, and corbelling was used to span drains and openings.

3. Public architecture

  • Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro: a tank of about 12 m × 7 m × 2.4 m, made watertight with a layer of bitumen, with steps at both ends and rooms around it, probably for ritual bathing.
  • Granaries: large structures at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, possibly for storing grain, though their function is debated.
  • Lothal "dockyard": a brick basin linked to a channel, interpreted as a dock (some see it as a water tank); Kalibangan and Lothal also had fire altars.
  • Dholavira: a chain of rock-cut reservoirs and a large open ground, showing skill in water management in arid Kutch.

4. Sanitation and water supply

  • Covered drainage: house drains joined brick-lined street drains with manholes and soak pits, among the most advanced systems of the Bronze Age world.
  • Water supply: Mohenjo-daro had several hundred wells; Dholavira stored rain and stream water in reservoirs.
  • Civic discipline: regular cleaning of drains points to some form of municipal authority.

The plan was not uniform everywhere, and in the late phase houses encroached on streets. Still, Harappan architecture combined standardisation, sanitation and civic order on a scale unmatched in its age; Dholavira's inscription as a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021) shows its lasting value for urban planning.
free.upm-2025-gs1-2:
Sulh-i-kulIbadat KhanaDin-i-IlahiComposite culture

Akbar (r. 1556–1605) moved from orthodox Sunni practice to a policy of sulh-i-kul ("peace with all"), described by his court historian Abul Fazl in the Akbarnama and the Ain-i-Akbari. His syncretism was both a personal search for truth and a strategy for ruling an empire in which Muslims were a minority. It blended Islamic, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian, Christian and Sufi ideas in policy, court ritual and culture.

1. Political and administrative aspects

  • Ending discrimination: Akbar abolished the pilgrim tax (1563) and the jizya on non-Muslims (1564), treating all subjects alike.
  • Rajput partnership: his marriage to the Kachhwaha princess of Amber (1562) began alliances that brought Rajputs such as Raja Man Singh into the highest ranks of the nobility, while non-Rajput Hindus such as Raja Todar Mal (a Khatri) headed the revenue administration.
  • Mahzar (1579): a declaration signed by leading ulema that allowed Akbar, as a just ruler, to decide between conflicting interpretations of Islamic law, reducing the hold of orthodox clerics.
  • Theory of kingship: Abul Fazl presented the emperor as receiving divine light (farr-i-izadi), a ruler above sectarian divisions and responsible for the welfare of all.

2. Dialogue among faiths

  • Ibadat Khana (1575): the House of Worship at Fatehpur Sikri, first for Sunni scholars, was opened from 1578 to Shias, Brahmins, Jains, Zoroastrians and Christians.
  • Wide contacts: Jesuit missions came from Goa (the first in 1580); the Jain monk Hiravijaya Suri and the Parsi priest Dastur Meherji Rana were honoured at court.
  • Translation bureau (Maktab Khana): the Mahabharata was rendered into Persian as the Razmnama, and the Ramayana and other Sanskrit works were translated, to make Indian traditions known to the Persian-reading elite.

3. Din-i-Ilahi and court culture

  • Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi, 1582): a discipleship order of nobles who pledged loyalty to the emperor, not a new religion; it had very few members, Birbal among them.
  • Ilahi era (1584): a solar calendar counted from his accession was adopted for official records.
  • Art and architecture: Fatehpur Sikri mixed Persian arches with Hindu brackets, chhajjas and chhatris; the Hamzanama paintings fused Persian and Indian styles.

4. Limitations

  • Orthodox opposition: Badauni criticised these policies in his Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh, and religious grievances fed the revolts in Bihar and Bengal (1580–81).
  • Elite and personal: the experiment stayed within the court and did not survive Akbar; Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679.
  • Political motive: historians debate how far it was conviction and how far a strategy to strengthen imperial authority.

Akbar's syncretism turned tolerance into a principle of governance. Though personal and short-lived, sulh-i-kul shaped a composite culture that anticipates the modern Indian idea of equal respect for all faiths.
free.upm-2025-gs2-1:
Corrupt practicesSection 123Undue influenceLok Prahari (2018)

The Representation of the People Act, 1951 lists corrupt practices in Section 123: acts by a candidate, his election agent or another person with their consent that destroy the voter's free choice. Proved in an election petition, they void the election (Section 100(1)(b)) and can lead to disqualification. In Lok Prahari v. Union of India (2018) the Supreme Court linked legislators' unexplained wealth to this framework.

1. Corrupt practices under Section 123

  • Bribery (Section 123(1)): any gift, offer or promise of gratification to make a person stand or not stand, withdraw, vote or refrain from voting.
  • Undue influence (Section 123(2)): any direct or indirect interference with the free exercise of an electoral right, such as threats of injury or social ostracism, or of divine displeasure.
  • Communal appeals (Section 123(3), (3A)): seeking votes on grounds of religion, race, caste, community or language, or promoting enmity; Abhiram Singh (2017) extended the bar to appeals to the voter's religion or caste.
  • Others: glorifying sati, false statements about a rival, free conveyance of voters, overspending, help from government servants and booth capturing.

2. Disproportionate assets: the Lok Prahari case

  • Non-disclosure is undue influence: on 16 February 2018 Justices J. Chelameswar and S. Abdul Nazeer held that hiding the assets and income sources of candidates and their associates is an attempt to "suppress, misguide and keep people in the dark", amounting to undue influence.
  • Unexplained wealth: where assets grow without relation to known income, "the only logical inference" is some abuse of the legislator's constitutional office, inconsistent with the rule of law.
  • Directions: nomination affidavits (Form 26) must disclose the income sources of the candidate, spouse and dependants; the Union never set up the asset-monitoring mechanism the Court sought, and the Court later found no contempt.

3. Analysis: is the wealth itself undue influence?

  • Not by itself: Section 123(2) targets interference with a voter's choice in an election; growth of assets during a term does not, on its own, interfere with any voter, and corrupt practices are quasi-criminal charges needing strict proof.
  • Concealment crosses the line: hiding or falsifying the wealth in Form 26 deceives voters, which Lok Prahari treats as undue influence; using such money to buy votes is bribery.
  • The right forum: a disproportionate rise is illicit enrichment under Section 13(1)(b) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, as legislators are public servants (P.V. Narasimha Rao, 1998); a conviction disqualifies under Section 8 of the RP Act.
  • False affidavits: Section 125A punishes them with up to six months' imprisonment but does not disqualify, a gap the Law Commission (244th Report, 2014) proposed to close.

Unexplained wealth is a symptom of corruption rather than, by itself, undue influence; its concealment is what vitiates an election. A statutory asset-monitoring mechanism and time-bound trial of election petitions would give the 2018 judgment real teeth.
free.upm-2025-gs2-2:
Articles 323A and 323BTribunalisationTribunals Reforms Act 2021National Tribunals Commission

Tribunals are specialised quasi-judicial bodies that decide disputes in fields such as service matters, tax, company law and the environment. The 42nd Amendment (1976), following the Swaran Singh Committee, inserted Articles 323A and 323B to let legislatures create them. The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 rationalised them but met repeated judicial objections, leading to a new law in 2026.

1. Why tribunals are needed alongside courts

  • Expertise: benches of judicial and technical members suit technical disputes, as in the National Green Tribunal (2010) or the NCLT and NCLAT under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
  • Speed and flexibility: they are not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure or strict rules of evidence, follow natural justice and can work to statutory time limits.
  • Relief to courts: moving service disputes to the Central Administrative Tribunal (1985) and tax appeals to the ITAT eases the load on High Courts.
  • Access and cost: less formal procedures and benches in many cities help litigants.
  • Supplements, not substitutes: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) made judicial review under Articles 226, 227 and 32 part of the basic structure, so tribunal orders can be challenged before a High Court.

2. Problems that prompted reform

  • Executive control: parent ministries fund, staff and appoint tribunals while also litigating before them.
  • Vacancies, short tenures and overlapping bodies delayed justice.
  • Earlier attempt: the Finance Act, 2017 merged tribunals (26 to 19), but Rojer Mathew (2019) struck down the rules framed under it.

3. The 2021 rationalisation and its impact

  • Abolition: bodies such as the Film Certification Appellate Tribunal, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and the Airport Appellate Tribunal were dissolved, and their work moved to High Courts and civil or commercial courts.
  • Uniform conditions: a four-year term, a minimum age of 50, and search-cum-selection committees chaired by the CJI or his nominee, with two Union Secretaries.
  • Burden shifted: High Courts received specialised cases without new judges; the Delhi High Court created an Intellectual Property Division (2021).
  • Clash over independence: the Act re-enacted provisions the Court had struck down in July 2021. In Madras Bar Association (19 November 2025) the Court struck down its appointment and tenure provisions and ordered a National Tribunals Commission within four months.
  • Response: the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 (assent 13 August, in force from 25 August 2026) set up a five-member National Tribunals Commission to oversee appointments, review performance, handle complaints against members and maintain a National Tribunals Data Grid for 16 tribunals; members get five-year terms (chairpersons up to 70, members up to 67).

Rationalisation has made the system leaner, but its impact depends on independence: an autonomous Commission, judicial primacy in selection and adequate staff would let tribunals deliver speedy, expert justice without diluting judicial review.
free.upm-2025-gs3-1:
Human Development IndexInequality-adjusted HDILoss due to inequalityInclusive growth

The Human Development Index (HDI), published by the UNDP since 1990 and built on the ideas of Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen, measures a country's average achievement in health, knowledge and standard of living. The Inequality-adjusted HDI (IHDI), introduced in the 2010 Human Development Report, discounts each of these averages for how unequally it is shared. The gap between the two, the "loss due to inequality", shows how far progress has failed to reach everyone.

1. HDI and IHDI distinguished

  • What HDI measures: it is the geometric mean of three indices: life expectancy at birth; mean and expected years of schooling; and gross national income per capita (PPP, log-scaled). It describes the "average" person.
  • What IHDI adds: it reduces each dimension's average by the inequality in its distribution across people, so it shows the human development of the "actual" person.
  • Relation between them: IHDI equals HDI only under perfect equality; otherwise it is lower, and the percentage gap is the loss due to inequality.

2. India's position

  • Steady progress: India's HDI reached 0.685 in HDR 2025 (rank 130 of 193), in the "medium" group and close to the 0.700 threshold of "high" human development; life expectancy rose to 72 years.
  • Large inequality loss: the IHDI of 0.475 means about 30.7% of India's human development is lost to inequality, one of the highest losses in the region (UNDP).
  • Where the gap lies: unequal incomes, uneven quality of schooling and health care across States, castes and rural–urban areas, and gender gaps; HDR 2025 notes that women's labour force participation and political representation lag behind.

3. Why the IHDI is a better indicator of inclusive growth

  • Distribution, not averages: inclusive growth means broad-based gains; IHDI falls when gains are concentrated among a few, even if GDP and HDI rise.
  • Pinpoints the weak dimension: it reports inequality separately for health, education and income, guiding targeted policy, for example on learning outcomes or out-of-pocket health spending.
  • "Leave no one behind": it matches SDG 10 (reduced inequalities) and Sen's capability approach, judging progress by what the actual person can do and be.
  • Tracks policy impact: a shrinking loss over time shows whether welfare programmes are spreading gains.

4. Limits of the IHDI

  • It does not show overlapping deprivations in the same household, which the Multidimensional Poverty Index captures; it does not separate caste, gender or regional gaps; and it relies on household surveys that lag.

The HDI tells us how far India has come; the IHDI tells us how many have come along. Narrowing the inequality loss through quality schooling, health care and decent jobs, especially for women, is the real test of inclusive growth on the road to Viksit Bharat 2047.
free.upm-2025-gs3-2:
ProtectionismBilateralismWTO crisisExport diversification

After decades of multilateral liberalisation under the WTO (1995), the world economy is turning to tariffs, industrial subsidies and one-to-one deals. The WTO's Appellate Body has been unable to hear appeals since December 2019, and in August 2025 the USA, India's largest export market, raised tariffs on most Indian goods to 50%. For India, which needs export-led manufacturing to become a developed nation by 2047, this shift brings serious challenges.

1. Challenges for the Indian economy

  • Tariff shocks: the 2025 US tariffs hit labour-intensive exports such as textiles, gems and jewellery and shrimp. The extra 25% "Russian oil" tariff was removed on 7 February 2026 and the reciprocal tariffs lapsed after the US Supreme Court ruling of 20 February 2026; a temporary 10% tariff on all countries followed, and in July 2026 the USA announced new 10% duties on about half of India's exports to it.
  • A weakened WTO: with no working Appellate Body and no agreement on agriculture at MC14 (Yaoundé, March 2026), India's food-stockholding programme and its right to fair dispute settlement are less secure.
  • Green and standards protectionism: the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (definitive phase from January 2026) taxes the carbon in steel, aluminium and cement exports; due-diligence rules raise compliance costs for MSMEs.
  • Trade diversion: goods shut out of Western markets, especially Chinese steel, chemicals and solar products, are dumped in India, hurting domestic producers.
  • Technology and services barriers: chip export controls and a steep US fee on new H-1B visa petitions (2025).
  • Unequal bargaining: in bilateral deals larger economies press for access to agriculture, dairy and data, sensitive areas for a country of small farmers.

2. How the challenges can be met

  • Smart bilateralism: a wider network of trade deals: the UAE CEPA and Australia ECTA (2022), the EFTA TEPA (in force October 2025), the UK CETA (signed July 2025), the Oman CEPA (signed December 2025), FTAs with New Zealand and the EU (announced December 2025 and January 2026), and a framework for an interim deal with the USA (February 2026), its first tranche still in legal drafting in October 2026.
  • Diversify markets and products: Africa, Latin America and ASEAN; electronics, pharmaceuticals, defence goods, and services through Global Capability Centres.
  • Competitiveness at home: PLI schemes, PM Gati Shakti and the National Logistics Policy (2022) to cut logistics costs; lower tariffs on inputs; simpler compliance for exporters.
  • Trade defence and standards: anti-dumping and safeguard duties through the DGTR, and quality standards against substandard imports.
  • Financial resilience: trade settlement in rupees (RBI, July 2022) and ample forex reserves.
  • Reform multilateralism: work with developing countries to restore the Appellate Body and secure a permanent solution on public stockholding, and use the G20 and BRICS to oppose unilateral tariffs.

India should neither retreat into protectionism nor depend on any one market. Strategic openness, combining competitive manufacturing, diversified FTAs and a strong voice for a rules-based WTO, can turn disruption into a larger share of global value chains.
free.upm-2025-gs4-1a:
Digital ethicsFree speech vs harmPrivacyAlgorithmic accountability

Social media has turned every user into a publisher and created a borderless digital public sphere. It has amplified unheard voices, helped in disasters and widened democratic debate. But the same features that make it powerful (speed, anonymity, virality and data-driven design) also create ethical dilemmas: situations in which two legitimate values, such as freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a) and protection from harm, pull in opposite directions.

1. Free expression vs harm to others

  • Speech vs hate and rumour: rumours of child-lifters spread on messaging apps led to mob lynchings in 2018; in Tehseen Poonawalla v UoI (2018) the Supreme Court asked governments to curb content that incites such violence. Yet over-zealous blocking chills legitimate dissent.
  • Who decides what is true? If platforms or governments remove content, they risk becoming censors; if they do nothing, falsehood outruns correction. In Shreya Singhal v UoI (2015) the Court struck down the vague Section 66A of the IT Act: limits on speech must be narrow and lawful.
  • Trial by social media: viral outrage can destroy reputations before facts are known, undermining the presumption of innocence.

2. Connectivity vs privacy

  • "Free" services paid for with data: platforms profit by profiling users for targeted advertising; the Cambridge Analytica scandal (2018) showed how harvested data can be used to influence voters.
  • Consent as a formality: long, opaque terms reduce consent to a click, although privacy is a fundamental right (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017). The DPDP Act, 2023, whose duties are being phased in under the DPDP Rules notified in November 2025, requires informed consent, but tension with state access to data remains.

3. Engagement vs well-being

  • Addictive design: infinite scroll, likes and autoplay are built to maximise screen time, raising concerns about anxiety, sleep loss and poor attention among adolescents.
  • Children: the DPDP Act requires verifiable parental consent for users under 18 and bars tracking and targeted advertising aimed at them; Australia has set a minimum age of 16 for social media accounts (from December 2025). The dilemma is protection versus autonomy and access to information.
  • Cyberbullying and trolling, especially of women and minorities, push people out of public debate.

4. Authenticity vs manipulation

  • Anonymity: it protects whistle-blowers and dissenters but also shields trolls, bots and fake accounts; tracing originators, in turn, threatens encryption and privacy.
  • Deepfakes: generative AI blurs truth and fiction; the IT Amendment Rules, 2026 (in force from 20 February 2026) require AI-generated ("synthetic") content to be labelled prominently, and complaints about non-consensual intimate or morphed images to be acted on within two hours.
  • Influencer ethics: paid promotions passed off as personal opinion deceive followers; the Department of Consumer Affairs' guidelines (January 2023) require influencers to disclose them.

The answer lies not in sacrificing one value for another but in balancing them through ethics by design, transparent algorithms, proportionate regulation and digital literacy, so that every user becomes a responsible digital citizen.
free.upm-2025-gs4-1b:
Constitutional moralityRule of lawGood governanceAccountability

Constitutional morality means respect for the core norms of the Constitution, not merely its text: the rule of law, liberty, equality and dignity. Introducing the Draft Constitution on 4 November 1948, Dr B.R. Ambedkar took the idea from the historian George Grote ("a paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution") and added, in his own words, that it "is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." The statement adds how: through civic education and adherence to the rule of law.

1. Meaning: why it must be cultivated

  • Beyond legality: an act may be legal yet violate the Constitution's spirit; constitutional morality guides where the text is silent.
  • Judicial articulation: in Manoj Narula v UoI (2014) the Supreme Court described it as bowing to the norms of the Constitution and not acting arbitrarily; in Navtej Singh Johar (2018) it held that constitutional morality prevails over majoritarian social morality.
  • How it is cultivated: civic education (Fundamental Duties under Article 51A), training of officials, and daily practice in which institutions keep within their limits.

2. Significance for the public servant

  • Loyalty to the Constitution, not to persons: the All India Services (Conduct) Rules, as amended in 2014, require officers to uphold the supremacy of the Constitution and democratic values, and to act with political neutrality.
  • Compass for discretion: non-arbitrariness is part of equality (E.P. Royappa, 1974); constitutional morality guides choices where rules leave room for judgement.
  • Protection of the vulnerable: it obliges officials to protect individual rights even against popular pressure, as in Shakti Vahini v UoI (2018), where the Court directed the police and district officials to protect couples threatened with "honour" crimes.
  • Moral courage: it helps the officer refuse illegal orders and give frank advice.

3. Role in promoting good governance

  • Rule of law and predictability: decisions follow law and due process, not whim; in its November 2024 judgment on demolitions, the Supreme Court held that the executive cannot act as judge and punish the accused by demolishing homes.
  • Equity and inclusion: the Directive Principles and Article 14 push administration towards the last citizen, not the most influential one.
  • Transparency and participation: proactive disclosure under the RTI Act, 2005, consultation and reasoned orders make governance open.

4. Role in ensuring accountability

  • Answerability to law and citizens: constitutional morality treats power as a trust; officials must explain their decisions to courts, the legislature (through the CAG and committees) and the public.
  • Natural justice: fair procedure (Maneka Gandhi, 1978) and speaking orders make decisions reviewable.
  • Limits on coercive power: safeguards on arrest and custody (D.K. Basu, 1997) show that even the state's strongest powers remain answerable.

Constitutional morality turns the Constitution from a legal document into a living ethic of administration. Cultivated through civic education, training and example, it makes the civil servant the guardian of a just and accountable state.
